title: Why is your WIFI snitching on you?
author: Ghassan Karian
summary: Ghassan Karian examines Kadence, a workplace platform that marks employees present simply because their device joins the office WiFi, and argues that its Hybrid Compliance module is surveillance dressed in the language of employee experience. He sets the managerial instinct to monitor against the evidence, citing the Bloom, Han and Liang randomised trial at Trip.com, where hybrid staff matched in-office staff on productivity and promotion while resigning 33% less, and a Pittsburgh study linking return-to-office mandates to higher turnover among the best people. He grants the charitable case, aggregated and anonymised occupancy data for space planning, but insists individual attendance tracking serves a different purpose, which is gathering ammunition about whether someone is pulling their weight. Covert data collection, he says, erodes the trust and openness that high-performing organisations depend on, and he points to UK regulator guidance and employee attitudes favouring disclosure. His conclusion is that reaching for WiFi tracking reveals a leadership team that has already decided against trust, so the return-to-office debate was about control rather than productivity.
points: Kadence's Hybrid Compliance module turns a passive WiFi connection into an individual attendance record, which Karian classes as surveillance rather than workforce insight.
The Trip.com randomised trial found zero productivity or promotion difference between hybrid and full-time office staff but a 33% drop in resignations.
Return-to-office mandates were followed by 14% higher turnover, concentrated among managers and top-skill employees, and slower hiring.
Aggregated occupancy data for space planning is legitimate, but tracking named individuals is aimed at building a case about them.
Leaders who reach for covert monitoring show that the trust question is already settled, and that the debate was always about control.
quotes: Let’s be brutally clear about what this is: it is surveillance infrastructure dressed up in the language of employee experience.

The findings were unambiguous and, for executives who had been assuming that full-time office presence improves output, uncomfortable: hybrid workers were exactly as productive as full-time in-office counterparts. Zero measurable performance difference.
The people most likely to leave when you demand full-time in-person attendance are your best people. They have the most options. They leave first and then you struggle replace them.
Nobody serious objects to organisations using aggregated, anonymised occupancy data to figure out whether they need six floors or four.
Put simply, they don’t trust their employees. They believe that without the data (without that sneaky surveillance of the WiFi check-in) people will work from home more than they should.

And surveillance, as the evidence on psychological safety consistently shows, destroys precisely the conditions (trust, openness, willingness to take risks) that high-performing organisations most need.

Instead, it starts with a dashboard and ends with a compliance metric. Which tells you something important: for the organisations that have turned Kadence into a covert attendance register, the return-to-office debate was never really about productivity. It was always about control.
